name: Arrhenius Activation Energy (Two-Point)
description: Determines the activation energy of a reaction from rate constants at two temperatures as R·ln(k2/k1)/(1/T1 - 1/T2). It uses the Arrhenius temperature dependence between two measured points.
notes: Temperatures must be absolute (kelvin) and the rate constants must share the same units. Assumes Arrhenius behavior with a temperature-independent activation energy over the interval.

name: Arrhenius Pre-exponential Factor
description: Recovers the Arrhenius pre-exponential (frequency) factor A as k·exp(Ea/(R·T)), inverting the Arrhenius equation from a measured rate constant, activation energy, and temperature.
notes: Temperature must be in kelvin and Ea and R in consistent energy units (J/mol and J/(mol·K)). The factor A carries the same units as the rate constant k.

name: Eyring Equation Rate Constant
description: Computes a reaction rate constant from transition-state theory via the Eyring equation as (kB·T/h)·exp(-dG/(R·T)), using the Gibbs energy of activation dG. It links molecular thermodynamics to reaction rate.
notes: Mixes molecular constants (kB, h) with the molar activation Gibbs energy and molar gas constant R, which is consistent here. Temperature is in kelvin; the transmission coefficient is assumed to be 1.

name: Mean Molecular Speed (Maxwell-Boltzmann)
description: Computes the mean (average) speed of gas molecules from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution as sqrt(8·R·T/(pi·M)), where M is the molar mass. It is the arithmetic average of molecular speeds at temperature T.
notes: Molar mass must be in kg/mol (not g/mol) and temperature in kelvin for a result in m/s. This mean speed is larger than the most probable speed but smaller than the RMS speed.

name: Root-Mean-Square Molecular Speed
description: Computes the root-mean-square speed of gas molecules as sqrt(3·R·T/M), the speed corresponding to the average kinetic energy of the molecules at temperature T.
notes: Molar mass must be in kg/mol and temperature in kelvin. The RMS speed is the largest of the three characteristic speeds and is what determines the average translational kinetic energy.

name: Most Probable Molecular Speed
description: Computes the most probable speed of gas molecules as sqrt(2·R·T/M), the speed at the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution at temperature T.
notes: Molar mass must be in kg/mol and temperature in kelvin. This is the smallest of the three characteristic speeds, below both the mean and RMS speeds.

name: Mean Free Path of Gas Molecules
description: Computes the mean free path of gas molecules as kB·T/(sqrt(2)·pi·d²·P), the average distance a molecule travels between collisions, given the molecular diameter d and pressure P.
notes: Uses a hard-sphere model; d is the collision diameter and temperature is in kelvin. The mean free path grows as pressure falls, becoming very large in a vacuum.

name: Collision Frequency (Single Molecule)
description: Computes how many collisions a single gas molecule undergoes per second as sqrt(2)·pi·d²·vbar·ndens, using the molecular diameter d, mean speed vbar, and number density ndens.
notes: Uses a hard-sphere model with number density in molecules per cubic meter. The sqrt(2) factor accounts for the relative motion of all molecules, not just the tracked one.

name: Boltzmann Population Ratio
description: Computes the population ratio of two nondegenerate energy levels as exp(-dE/(kB·T)), the Boltzmann factor giving the relative occupancy of the upper level compared with the lower one.
notes: dE is the energy gap in joules and temperature is in kelvin; the result is dimensionless and always between 0 and 1. This form assumes both levels have equal degeneracy.

name: Boltzmann Population Ratio (with Degeneracy)
description: Computes the population ratio of two energy levels including their degeneracies as (g2/g1)·exp(-dE/(kB·T)), scaling the Boltzmann factor by the ratio of statistical weights.
notes: g1 and g2 are the number of states at each level; unlike the simple form, this ratio can exceed 1 when the upper level is more degenerate. Energy is in joules and temperature in kelvin.

name: Translational Partition Function
description: Computes the translational partition function of a gas particle as V·(2·pi·m·kB·T/h²)^1.5, counting the number of thermally accessible translational quantum states in a volume V.
notes: m is the mass of a single molecule in kg and V is in cubic meters; temperature is in kelvin. The large dimensionless result reflects the enormous number of accessible states.

name: Van der Waals Pressure
description: Computes the pressure of a real gas from the van der Waals equation as n·R·T/(V - n·b) - a·n²/V², correcting the ideal gas law for molecular volume (b) and intermolecular attraction (a).
notes: Constants a and b are gas-specific and must match the SI unit system used here. The excluded-volume term requires V greater than n·b; the model breaks down near the critical point.

name: Redlich-Kwong Pressure
description: Computes real-gas pressure from the Redlich-Kwong equation of state as R·T/(Vm - b) - a/(sqrt(T)·Vm·(Vm + b)), an improvement over van der Waals with a temperature-dependent attraction term.
notes: Vm is the molar volume and the RK constants a and b are gas-specific; the attraction term scales with 1/sqrt(T). Requires Vm greater than b and works best at moderate pressures.

name: Compressibility Factor
description: Computes the compressibility factor Z of a gas as P·Vm/(R·T), the ratio of the real molar volume to that predicted by the ideal gas law. It measures deviation from ideal behavior.
notes: Z equals 1 for an ideal gas; below 1 indicates dominant attraction, above 1 indicates dominant repulsion. Pressure in pascals, molar volume in m³/mol, and temperature in kelvin.

name: Virial Equation of State (Second Coefficient)
description: Computes the compressibility factor using the pressure-form virial equation truncated at the second coefficient as 1 + B·P/(R·T), where B is the second virial coefficient capturing pairwise molecular interactions.
notes: Valid at low to moderate pressures where higher virial terms are negligible; B is temperature-dependent and can be negative. Pressure is in pascals and temperature in kelvin.

name: Joule-Thomson Coefficient (van der Waals)
description: Estimates the Joule-Thomson coefficient of a van der Waals gas as (2·a/(R·T) - b)/Cp, the temperature change per unit pressure drop during throttling. Its sign shows whether the gas cools or warms on expansion.
notes: Uses van der Waals constants a and b with molar heat capacity Cp; the inversion temperature is where the numerator changes sign. Result is in K/Pa with all quantities in SI units.

name: Clausius-Clapeyron Enthalpy of Vaporization
description: Estimates the molar enthalpy of vaporization of a liquid from two vapor pressures measured at two temperatures, using the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation. The result quantifies the energy required to vaporize one mole of the substance.
notes: Assumes constant enthalpy of vaporization over the range and ideal vapor obeying the ideal gas law. Temperatures must be absolute (K); P1/P2 need only be in consistent units since their ratio is used.

name: Kelvin Equation (Droplet Vapor Pressure Ratio)
description: Gives the ratio of the vapor pressure over a small curved liquid droplet to that over a flat surface, from the Kelvin equation. A value above 1 shows that smaller droplets have a higher equilibrium vapor pressure due to surface curvature.
notes: The radius is positive for a convex droplet, giving a ratio greater than 1; use a negative radius for a concave meniscus. All inputs must be in SI units so the exponent is dimensionless.

name: Young-Laplace Pressure (Droplet)
description: Calculates the Laplace pressure, the excess internal pressure inside a spherical droplet or bubble caused by surface tension, as twice the surface tension divided by the radius. Smaller droplets sustain a larger pressure difference across their surface.
notes: This 2·gamma/r form is for a spherical liquid droplet with a single interface; a soap bubble with two surfaces requires 4·gamma/r. Use SI units for a result in pascals.

name: Capillary Rise Height (Jurin's Law)
description: Computes the height a liquid rises (or falls) in a narrow capillary tube by Jurin's law, balancing surface tension against gravity. The rise increases for higher surface tension and smaller tube radius.
notes: The contact angle theta is in radians; theta=0 means perfect wetting. A contact angle above 90 degrees (cos negative) gives a capillary depression. Uses the tube inner radius, not diameter.

name: Langmuir Adsorption Isotherm (Fractional Coverage)
description: Gives the fractional surface coverage of adsorbed molecules as a function of pressure from the Langmuir isotherm. The value ranges from 0 to 1, approaching 1 (full monolayer) as pressure rises.
notes: Assumes a single adsorption layer, equivalent independent sites, and no interaction between adsorbed molecules. The product K·P must be dimensionless, so K and P must use reciprocal pressure units.

name: Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm
description: Computes the amount adsorbed per unit mass of adsorbent as an empirical power function of the equilibrium concentration, following the Freundlich isotherm. Larger Kf and concentration increase the adsorbed amount.
notes: This is an empirical relation with no saturation limit, valid over a limited concentration range. The intensity factor nf is greater than 1 for favorable adsorption; the exponent is 1/nf.

name: Osmotic Pressure (van't Hoff Factor)
description: Calculates the osmotic pressure of a dilute solution from the van't Hoff equation, including the van't Hoff factor i to account for solute dissociation. Pressure rises with concentration, temperature, and the number of particles per formula unit.
notes: Valid for dilute ideal solutions; use i near the number of ions produced (i=2 for NaCl). Keep R consistent with the units: with R=0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) the result is in atm and T in kelvin.

name: Boiling Point Elevation (van't Hoff Factor)
description: Computes how much a solvent's boiling point rises when a solute is dissolved, from the molality, the ebullioscopic constant, and the van't Hoff factor. The elevation is a colligative property depending on particle concentration.
notes: Use molality (mol solute per kg solvent), not molarity. The van't Hoff factor i counts dissolved particles (i=2 for a fully dissociating 1:1 salt); the result is a temperature difference in kelvin.

name: Freezing Point Depression (van't Hoff Factor)
description: Computes how much a solvent's freezing point drops when a solute is dissolved, from the molality, the cryoscopic constant, and the van't Hoff factor. This colligative lowering depends on the number of dissolved particles.
notes: Use molality (mol per kg solvent), not molarity. The factor i counts dissolved particles (i=2 for NaCl); the result is the magnitude of the temperature drop in kelvin, subtracted from the pure freezing point.

name: Vapor Pressure Lowering (Raoult)
description: Gives the reduction in a solvent's vapor pressure caused by a nonvolatile solute, as the solute mole fraction times the pure solvent's vapor pressure, following Raoult's law. More solute lowers the vapor pressure further.
notes: Valid for ideal solutions with a nonvolatile solute; xsolute is the solute mole fraction (0 to 1), not a percentage. The result is the pressure decrease, in the same units as the pure solvent pressure.

name: Henry's Law Solubility
description: Calculates the equilibrium dissolved concentration of a gas in a liquid as the product of the Henry's law constant and the gas partial pressure. Higher partial pressure gives proportionally greater solubility.
notes: This concentration form of Henry's law needs a solubility-type constant; the constant is temperature dependent and gas solubility usually decreases as temperature rises. Keep kH and Pg units consistent with the desired concentration unit.

name: Debye-Hückel Limiting Law (Activity Coefficient)
description: Estimates the mean ionic activity coefficient of a dilute electrolyte from the Debye-Hückel limiting law, using ionic charges and ionic strength. The coefficient falls below 1 as ionic strength grows, reflecting ion-ion interactions.
notes: Valid only for very dilute solutions (ionic strength below about 0.01 mol/L). Use the magnitudes of the ion charges; A is about 0.509 for water at 25 degrees C. The result is the mean activity coefficient.

name: Extended Debye-Hückel Activity Coefficient
description: Estimates an ion's activity coefficient using the extended Debye-Hückel equation, which adds an ion-size term in the denominator to extend validity to higher ionic strength than the limiting law. The coefficient decreases with ionic strength.
notes: Valid up to about 0.1 mol/L ionic strength. The ion-size parameter is in ångström and must match B's units; use the magnitude of the ion charge. Beyond this range, add empirical extensions such as the Davies equation.

name: pH of Weak Acid (Approximation)
description: Estimates the pH of a weak monoprotic acid solution using the simple approximation that the hydrogen ion concentration equals the square root of Ka times the acid concentration. Lower pH means a stronger or more concentrated acid.
notes: Valid only when dissociation is small (Ca much greater than Ka) and the acid is not too dilute, so autoionization of water is negligible. It ignores the change in acid concentration due to dissociation.

name: pOH of Weak Base (Approximation)
description: Estimates the pOH of a weak base solution using the approximation that the hydroxide ion concentration equals the square root of Kb times the base concentration. The pH then follows as 14 minus this pOH at 25 degrees C.
notes: Valid only when dissociation is small (Cb much greater than Kb) and the base is not too dilute. To get pH, subtract the pOH from 14 (the value of pKw at 25 degrees C).

name: Buffer Capacity (van Slyke)
description: Computes the buffer capacity, the resistance of a buffer to pH change, from the van Slyke expression using total buffer concentration, Ka, and hydrogen ion concentration. Capacity is greatest when the pH equals the pKa.
notes: This term covers only the buffer component; near very low or high pH the contributions of H+ and OH- must be added. Capacity peaks at H equal to Ka (pH = pKa) and scales with total buffer concentration.

name: Isoelectric Point (pI)
description: Calculates the isoelectric point (pI) of an amphoteric species, such as an amino acid, as the average of the two pKa values that bracket the neutral zwitterionic form. At this pH the molecule carries no net charge.
notes: Use the two pKa values that flank the neutral (zwitterion) species. For amino acids with an ionizable side chain, choose the correct pair of pKa values rather than simply the alpha groups.

name: Ostwald Dilution Law (Degree of Dissociation)
description: Computes the degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte using the exact quadratic solution of Ostwald's dilution law, from the dissociation constant and concentration. The value ranges from 0 to 1 and rises as the solution is diluted.
notes: This full quadratic form avoids the small-dissociation approximation and stays valid even at low concentration. Ka and C must use consistent concentration units; the result is a dimensionless fraction.

name: Van't Hoff Reaction Isotherm
description: Calculates the Gibbs free energy change of a reaction under non-standard conditions from the standard Gibbs energy and the reaction quotient, using the van't Hoff reaction isotherm. A negative result indicates a spontaneous forward reaction.
notes: The reaction quotient Q is dimensionless (activities relative to standard states); at equilibrium Q equals K and the result is zero. Use absolute temperature and keep dG0 and R·T in the same energy units.

name: Van't Hoff Isochore (Reaction Enthalpy)
description: Estimates the standard reaction enthalpy from equilibrium constants measured at two temperatures, using the integrated van't Hoff isochore. A positive result indicates an endothermic reaction whose equilibrium constant rises with temperature.
notes: Assumes the reaction enthalpy is constant between the two temperatures. Temperatures must be absolute (K); the equilibrium constants are dimensionless and only their ratio K2/K1 enters the formula.

name: Kirchhoff's Law (Enthalpy Temperature Dependence)
description: Computes a reaction enthalpy at a new temperature from its value at a reference temperature, using Kirchhoff's law with the heat capacity change of the reaction. It corrects the enthalpy for the temperature difference between the two states.
notes: Assumes the heat capacity change dCp is constant over the temperature interval and that no phase transition occurs within it. Temperatures must be absolute (K); dCp is products minus reactants heat capacity.

name: Entropy of Mixing (Ideal, Binary)
description: Calculates the molar entropy of mixing for an ideal binary mixture from the two mole fractions. The result is always positive, reaching its maximum when the two components are present in equal amounts.
notes: The two mole fractions should sum to 1 and each lie between 0 and 1. Assumes ideal mixing with no enthalpy change; the result is per mole of total mixture in J/(mol·K).

name: Gibbs Energy of Mixing (Ideal, Binary)
description: Calculates the molar Gibbs free energy of mixing for an ideal binary mixture from temperature and the two mole fractions. The result is always negative, showing that ideal mixing is spontaneous.
notes: The two mole fractions should sum to 1, each between 0 and 1; temperature must be absolute (K). Assumes ideal mixing (zero enthalpy of mixing), so the whole effect is entropic.

name: Clapeyron Equation (Phase Boundary Slope)
description: Computes the slope of a phase-coexistence boundary in a pressure-temperature diagram, dP/dT, from the transition enthalpy, temperature, and molar volume change, using the exact Clapeyron equation. It applies to any first-order phase transition.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (K); dV is the molar volume change of the transition and can be negative (e.g. melting of ice), flipping the slope's sign. Use consistent SI units for a result in Pa/K.

name: Trouton's Rule (Entropy of Vaporization)
description: Computes the molar entropy of vaporization as the enthalpy of vaporization divided by the normal boiling point. Trouton's rule notes that this value is roughly 85-88 J/(mol·K) for many non-associating liquids.
notes: The boiling point must be absolute (K). The empirical rule breaks down for liquids with strong hydrogen bonding or molecular association (e.g. water, alcohols), which deviate above the typical value.

name: Arrhenius Rate Constant Ratio (k2/k1)
description: Calculates the ratio of rate constants at two different temperatures (k2/k1) from the activation energy, using the Arrhenius equation. It shows how strongly a reaction rate depends on temperature.
notes: Assumes the pre-exponential factor A is constant over the temperature range considered and that Ea does not vary with temperature. Use R and Ea in consistent energy units (e.g., both in J/mol, or both in cal/mol).

name: Nernst Equation (General, n Electrons)
description: Calculates the actual electrode or cell potential under non-standard conditions from the standard potential and reaction quotient, using the Nernst equation for a reaction transferring n electrons. Concentration deviations from standard shift the potential.
notes: The reaction quotient Q is dimensionless (activities); temperature must be absolute (K). More electrons transferred reduce the concentration term's influence. At equilibrium Q equals K and the potential is zero.

name: Concentration Cell EMF
description: Computes the electromotive force of a concentration cell, which generates voltage solely from a difference in ion concentration between two identical electrodes. The EMF grows with the concentration ratio between cathode and anode sides.
notes: The standard potential is zero because both electrodes are identical, so voltage arises only from the concentration ratio. Temperature must be absolute (K); the cell drives ions until the two concentrations equalize.

name: Cell Potential from Gibbs Energy
description: Calculates the cell potential from the Gibbs free energy change of the reaction, dividing by the number of electrons transferred times the Faraday constant. A negative Gibbs energy (spontaneous reaction) gives a positive cell potential.
notes: Use the Gibbs energy per mole of reaction and match n to the electrons transferred in the balanced equation. In SI units (J/mol and C/mol) the potential comes out in volts.

name: Faraday's Law (Mass Electrodeposited)
description: Computes the mass of substance deposited or dissolved at an electrode from the total charge passed, using Faraday's law of electrolysis with the molar mass and electrons per ion. More charge deposits proportionally more material.
notes: Match n to the electrons needed per ion (e.g. n=2 for Cu2+). Keep molar mass in kg/mol and charge in coulombs for a result in kilograms; charge equals current times time.

name: Faraday's Law (Mass from Current and Time)
description: Computes the mass deposited at an electrode directly from the current and electrolysis time via Faraday's law, since charge equals current times time. Higher current or longer time deposits proportionally more substance.
notes: Current in amperes and time in seconds give charge in coulombs; use molar mass in kg/mol for a result in kilograms. Set n to the electrons required per ion and assume 100 percent current efficiency.

name: Moles from Charge (Faraday)
description: Calculates the moles of substance reacted at an electrode from the total charge passed, dividing by the electrons per ion times the Faraday constant. It converts electric charge into a chemical amount of substance.
notes: Charge in coulombs (current times time) and n as the electrons per ion give moles directly. This assumes 100 percent current efficiency, with all charge going into the intended electrode reaction.

name: Charge Required for Electrolysis
description: Computes the total electric charge needed to electrolyze a given amount of substance, as the electrons per ion times the Faraday constant times the moles. It is the inverse of finding moles from charge.
notes: Set n to the electrons required per ion or molecule in the electrode reaction; the result is in coulombs. Dividing by a chosen current gives the required electrolysis time, at 100 percent efficiency.

name: Gas Volume Evolved in Electrolysis (STP)
description: Computes the volume of gas evolved at an electrode during electrolysis at STP, combining Faraday's law with the molar gas volume. It converts the charge passed into moles of gas and then into a volume.
notes: The molar volume used sets the reference conditions (about 0.0224 m^3/mol at STP); n is the electrons per gas molecule produced. Real gas volumes depend on the actual temperature and pressure.

name: Electrochemical Equivalent
description: Computes the electrochemical equivalent, the mass of a substance deposited or liberated per unit of electric charge, as the molar mass divided by electrons per ion times the Faraday constant. It characterizes how much material a given charge produces.
notes: With molar mass in kg/mol the result is in kg/C. Multiplying by the total charge passed gives the deposited mass. The value depends on the number of electrons per ion for the electrode reaction.

name: Faradaic (Current) Efficiency
description: Computes the faradaic (current) efficiency as the ratio of the actually deposited mass to the theoretical mass predicted by Faraday's law for the charge passed. A value near 1 means nearly all charge went into the intended reaction.
notes: Keep the actual mass and molar mass in matching mass units (both kg) so the result is a dimensionless fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Values below 1 indicate side reactions consumed charge.

name: Butler-Volmer Current Density
description: Computes the net electrode current density as a function of overpotential using the Butler-Volmer equation, combining the anodic and cathodic reaction rates. Current rises sharply and nonlinearly as the overpotential moves away from equilibrium.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (K) and overpotential in volts; at zero overpotential the net current is zero. The anodic and cathodic transfer coefficients typically sum to n for a single-step reaction.

name: Tafel Equation (Overpotential)
description: Estimates the overpotential needed to drive a given current density at an electrode using the Tafel equation, valid in the high-overpotential regime where one reaction direction dominates. Overpotential grows logarithmically with the current density ratio.
notes: Valid only far from equilibrium (current density well above the exchange current density i0). Temperature must be absolute (K); the base-10 logarithm of i/i0 is used, and i and i0 must share the same units.

name: Tafel Slope
description: Computes the Tafel slope, the increase in overpotential per tenfold (decade) increase in current density, from temperature and the electrode kinetics parameters. A smaller slope indicates faster electrode kinetics.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (K); the result is in volts per decade of current density. A common room-temperature value is about 0.12 V/decade for a one-electron step with a transfer coefficient of 0.5.

name: Diffusion-Limited Current Density
description: Computes the maximum (limiting) current density at an electrode set by the rate of diffusion of reactant across a stagnant diffusion layer of given thickness. It marks the current ceiling when the surface reactant concentration falls to zero.
notes: Use SI units, with bulk concentration in mol/m^3 and diffusion layer thickness in metres, for a result in A/m^2. A thinner diffusion layer (e.g. from stirring) raises the limiting current.

name: Cottrell Equation (Diffusion Current)
description: Computes the diffusion-controlled current at a planar electrode after a potential step as a function of time, using the Cottrell equation. The current decays in proportion to one over the square root of time.
notes: Valid for a planar electrode under pure semi-infinite linear diffusion, with no convection. Use consistent SI units; the current diverges as time approaches zero and decays steadily thereafter.

name: Randles-Sevcik Peak Current
description: Computes the peak current of a reversible redox couple in cyclic voltammetry at 25 degrees C using the Randles-Sevcik equation. The peak current scales with the square root of the scan rate and with concentration.
notes: The numerical prefactor 269000 fixes the units: use area in cm^2, diffusion coefficient in cm^2/s, concentration in mol/cm^3, and scan rate in V/s. It applies to a reversible process at about 25 degrees C.

name: Ionic Mobility from Molar Conductivity
description: Computes the mobility of an ion, its drift velocity per unit electric field, from its molar ionic conductivity divided by the charge number times the Faraday constant. Higher molar conductivity implies a more mobile ion.
notes: Use the magnitude of the ion charge number. With molar conductivity in S·m^2/mol and F in C/mol, the mobility comes out in m^2/(V·s). It reflects the ion in a specific solvent at a specific temperature.

name: Nernst-Einstein Equation (Ionic Diffusion)
description: Computes the diffusion coefficient of an ion from its ionic mobility using the Nernst-Einstein relation, linking electrical transport to thermal diffusion. Higher mobility and temperature give a larger diffusion coefficient.
notes: Use the magnitude of the ion charge number and absolute temperature (K); all SI units give a diffusion coefficient in m^2/s. It assumes dilute, ideal behavior with no ion-ion correlations.

name: Einstein Relation (Diffusion-Mobility)
description: Computes the diffusion coefficient of a charged particle from its electrical mobility using the Einstein-Smoluchowski relation, expressed with the Boltzmann constant and single-particle charge. It connects random thermal motion to field-driven drift.
notes: This single-particle form uses the Boltzmann constant and elementary charge q, unlike the molar Nernst-Einstein form. Temperature must be absolute (K); all SI units give a result in m^2/s.

name: Molar Conductivity
description: Computes the molar conductivity of an electrolyte solution as its measured conductivity divided by concentration. It normalizes conductivity per mole of electrolyte, allowing comparison across different concentrations.
notes: Keep units consistent: conductivity in S/m and concentration in mol/m^3 give molar conductivity in S·m^2/mol. Molar conductivity generally rises with dilution as ion interactions weaken.

name: Kohlrausch's Law (Molar Conductivity)
description: Estimates the molar conductivity of a strong electrolyte at a given concentration from Kohlrausch's law, which subtracts a term proportional to the square root of concentration from the limiting molar conductivity. Conductivity decreases as concentration rises.
notes: Valid for strong electrolytes in dilute solution only. Keep the concentration unit consistent with the Kohlrausch coefficient Kc; the result approaches the limiting value as concentration approaches zero.

name: Transport Number (Cation)
description: Computes the cation transport number, the fraction of the total electric current carried by the cation, from the cation and anion molar conductivities. The value lies between 0 and 1 and reflects the cation's relative mobility.
notes: The cation and anion transport numbers sum to 1, so the anion fraction is one minus this result. Both conductivities must be in the same units; their ratio is what determines the fraction.

name: Equilibrium Constant from Standard Cell Potential
description: Computes the equilibrium constant of a redox reaction from its standard cell potential, electrons transferred, and temperature, by inverting the relation between standard Gibbs energy and cell potential. A larger positive potential gives an exponentially larger equilibrium constant.
notes: Use the standard cell potential in volts and absolute temperature (K); match n to the electrons in the balanced reaction. The exponential form means the result grows extremely fast with potential.

name: pH from Hydrogen Electrode Potential
description: Estimates the pH of a solution from the measured potential of a hydrogen electrode, inverting the Nernst relation for the hydrogen half-reaction. A more negative potential corresponds to a higher (more alkaline) pH.
notes: Assumes a standard hydrogen electrode at 1 bar H2 and unit reference, with potential measured against it in volts. Temperature must be absolute (K); the 2.303 factor converts the natural log to base 10.

name: Liquid Junction Potential
description: Computes the liquid junction potential that develops across the boundary between two electrolyte solutions of different concentration, driven by unequal cation and anion mobilities. The size and sign depend on the difference in transport numbers and the concentration ratio.
notes: Uses a simplified single-electrolyte model; the transport numbers should sum to 1. Temperature must be absolute (K). The potential vanishes when cation and anion transport numbers are equal.

name: Theoretical Specific Capacity
description: Computes the maximum charge an electrode material can store per gram, converting n electrons per formula unit times the Faraday constant into mAh/g by dividing by molar mass M and the factor 3.6. The result sets the upper limit of a battery material's gravimetric capacity.
notes: The factor 3.6 converts C/g to mAh/g. Use molar mass in g/mol and n as the number of electrons exchanged per formula unit; real cells reach only a fraction of this theoretical value.

name: Peukert's Law (Battery Discharge Time)
description: Estimates how long a lead-acid battery lasts at a given discharge current I, using Peukert's law. It scales the rated discharge time H by the ratio of rated capacity to actual draw, raised to the Peukert exponent kp, so heavier loads shorten runtime more than linearly.
notes: kp is typically 1.1 to 1.3; kp=1 gives ideal behavior. Capacity Cap and current I must use consistent units (Ah and A) and H is the discharge time at which Cap is rated.

name: Coulombic Efficiency
description: Gives the ratio of charge extracted during discharge to charge injected during the preceding charge, Qd divided by Qc. It measures how reversibly a battery stores charge in one cycle, with values near 1 indicating minimal side reactions or capacity loss.
notes: Both charges must come from the same cycle and share units; the result is a dimensionless fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Values above 1 usually signal measurement error or parasitic reactions.

name: Battery Specific Energy
description: Calculates the energy stored per unit mass of a cell as cell voltage Vcell times charge capacity Q divided by cell mass m. It expresses how much usable energy a battery delivers relative to its weight, a key metric for portable and mobile applications.
notes: Charge Q here is in coulombs, so voltage times Q gives joules; divide by mass in kg for J/kg. To get Wh/kg, divide the result by 3600. Vcell should be an average operating voltage.

name: Concentration Overpotential
description: Computes the extra voltage needed to drive an electrode reaction when reactant depletion near the surface limits the current. It grows without bound as the current density i approaches the limiting value iL, reflecting mass-transport limitation.
notes: Requires i less than iL; at i equal to iL the logarithm diverges. Current densities i and iL must share units and T is the absolute temperature in kelvin.

name: Reaction Entropy from Cell Temperature Coefficient
description: Determines the entropy change of a cell reaction from the temperature dependence of its cell potential, as n times the Faraday constant times dE/dT. It links a measurable voltage-temperature slope to the reaction's thermodynamic entropy.
notes: dEdT is the temperature coefficient of the reversible cell potential in V/K and may be negative. The result is per mole of reaction as written for n transferred electrons.

name: Reaction Enthalpy from Cell Potential
description: Calculates the enthalpy change of a cell reaction from the cell potential and its temperature coefficient, as minus n times the Faraday constant times (Ecell minus T times dE/dT). It combines the Gibbs energy and entropy terms into the total reaction heat content.
notes: dEdT is in V/K and T is absolute temperature in kelvin; a negative result means an exothermic reaction. Use consistent sign conventions for n and Ecell.

name: Electrophoretic Mobility (Smoluchowski)
description: Gives the electrophoretic mobility of a charged particle in the Smoluchowski limit as permittivity times zeta potential divided by viscosity. It predicts how fast a particle drifts per unit applied electric field in a liquid.
notes: Valid when the particle is much larger than the electric double-layer thickness (thin double layer). Permittivity eps is the medium's absolute permittivity, not relative; a negative zeta gives migration toward the anode.

name: Corrosion Rate (Faraday's Law)
description: Estimates the rate at which a metal surface recedes due to corrosion from the corrosion current I, using Faraday's law. It converts the electrochemical dissolution current into a linear penetration rate through molar mass, density, valence n, and area A.
notes: Molar mass M is in kg/mol and density rho in kg/m^3 to give m/s; multiply by suitable factors for mm/year. Assumes uniform corrosion over the whole area A with n electrons per dissolved atom.

name: Donnan Membrane Potential
description: Computes the equilibrium electric potential difference across a membrane permeable to an ion of charge z, from the Nernst-type ratio of its outside to inside concentrations. It describes the potential arising when fixed charges restrict one ionic species.
notes: z carries sign; the concentration ratio cout/cin is dimensionless, so any consistent concentration unit works. T is absolute temperature in kelvin and the result is the outside-minus-inside potential.

name: Exchange Current Density
description: Calculates the exchange current density at equilibrium as n times the Faraday constant times the standard rate constant k0 times the reactant concentration C. It quantifies the intrinsic rate of forward and backward electron transfer when no net current flows.
notes: Uses concentration in mol/m^3 and k0 in m/s to give A/m^2; a higher exchange current density means faster, more reversible electrode kinetics. This simplified form assumes equal reactant and product concentrations.

name: Warburg Coefficient
description: Computes the Warburg coefficient governing diffusion-limited impedance in electrochemical systems, from temperature, transferred electrons n, electrode area A, diffusion coefficient D, and concentration C. It sets the magnitude of the low-frequency Warburg impedance in EIS analysis.
notes: The impedance it scales varies as the inverse square root of frequency, hence the units Ω·s^-0.5. Use SI units throughout; C is the bulk concentration of the diffusing species in mol/m^3.

name: Levich Equation (Rotating Disk Current)
description: Gives the mass-transport-limited current at a rotating disk electrode via the Levich equation, scaling with the square root of the angular rotation rate omega. It predicts the plateau current controlled by convective diffusion of reactant to the spinning electrode.
notes: The classic form uses CGS units (cm, cm^2/s, mol/cm^3) with the 0.62 prefactor; keep D, nu, A and C in those units. Current rises with the square root of rotation speed, a hallmark diagnostic of diffusion control.

name: Electrolyte Solution Resistance
description: Calculates the ohmic resistance of an electrolyte between two electrodes as the electrode separation L divided by the product of conductivity kappa and cross-sectional area A. It is the geometric resistance that governs IR drop in the solution.
notes: Assumes a uniform column of electrolyte with parallel electrodes of area A separated by L. Conductivity kappa is in S/m; higher concentration or temperature typically raises kappa and lowers resistance.

name: Electrolyte Conductivity from Ionic Mobilities
description: Computes the conductivity of a symmetric electrolyte as the Faraday constant times concentration times the sum of cation and anion mobilities. It links the microscopic drift mobilities of the ions to the bulk ability of the solution to carry current.
notes: Assumes a 1:1 electrolyte fully dissociated with concentration c in mol/m^3 and mobilities in m^2/(V·s). Mobilities here are magnitudes, so both cation and anion terms add positively.

name: Electrodeposit Thickness (Faraday)
description: Determines the thickness of a metal layer deposited by electroplating from Faraday's law, using current I, time t, molar mass, valence n, density, and deposit area A. It converts the total charge passed into a uniform coating thickness.
notes: Assumes 100 percent current efficiency and even deposition over area A. Molar mass M is in kg/mol and density in kg/m^3 to give meters; real efficiency lowers the actual thickness.

name: Zero-Order Concentration
description: Gives the concentration in a zero-order reaction, which falls in a straight line until it runs out.
notes: Alcohol elimination in the body is roughly zero order.

name: Zero-Order Half-Life
description: Gives the half-life of a zero-order reaction; unlike first order it is proportional to the starting concentration.
notes: Doubling the dose doubles the time to halve it.

name: Half-Life of an n-th Order Reaction
description: Gives the half-life of a reaction of any order n other than 1 (use ln 2/k for first order).
notes: For n = 2 it reduces to 1/(k·c₀).

name: Rate Change for a Temperature Rise (Arrhenius)
description: Gives how many times faster a reaction runs at T₂ than at T₁ for a given activation energy, with temperatures in °C.
notes: 50 kJ/mol roughly doubles the rate per 10 °C near room temperature.

name: Vapour Composition over an Ideal Mixture
description: Gives the mole fraction of component 1 in the vapour above an ideal liquid mixture (Raoult + Dalton); the vapour is richer in the more volatile component.
notes: The basis of distillation.

name: Equilibrium Curve with Constant Relative Volatility

variables.label: Liquid mole fraction of the light component

description: Gives the vapour composition in equilibrium with a liquid for a binary mixture of constant relative volatility — the McCabe–Thiele equilibrium line.
notes: α close to 1 means hard separation.

name: Minimum Number of Stages (Fenske)
description: Gives the fewest theoretical stages a distillation column needs, at total reflux (Fenske 1932).
notes: Real columns need about twice this at practical reflux.

name: CSTR Conversion (First Order)
description: Gives the fraction converted in a continuous stirred-tank reactor for a first-order reaction.
notes: A plug-flow reactor of the same size converts more: 1 − e^(−kτ).

name: Plug-Flow Reactor Conversion (First Order)
description: Gives the conversion in an ideal plug-flow (tubular) reactor for a first-order reaction.
notes: Also the conversion of a batch reactor after the same time.

name: Damköhler Number (First Order)
description: Compares reaction speed with flow-through time; Da ≫ 1 means the reaction finishes inside the reactor.
notes: Conversion in a CSTR is Da/(1 + Da).

name: Single-Stage Extraction Fraction Remaining
description: Gives the fraction of solute left in the original phase after one liquid–liquid extraction.
notes: Several small extractions beat one large one.

name: Multiple Extractions Fraction Remaining
description: Gives the fraction left after splitting the same solvent into n equal extractions.
notes: Three portions leave 22 % here against 33 % for one.

name: Filter Cake Filtration Time (Constant Pressure)
expression: mu * alf * cs / (2 * a^2 * dp) * v^2 + mu * rm / (a * dp) * v
description: Gives the time to collect a filtrate volume in constant-pressure cake filtration (Ruth equation).
notes: Time grows with the square of volume as the cake thickens.

name: Stoichiometric Air–Fuel Ratio of a Hydrocarbon
description: Gives the mass of air needed to burn one kilogram of a hydrocarbon CₓHᵧ completely.
notes: Octane gives about 15.1; methane about 17.2.

name: Higher Heating Value from Composition (Dulong)
description: Estimates the gross calorific value of coal or another solid fuel from its elemental analysis (Dulong).
notes: Hydrogen already bound to the fuel's oxygen does not burn — hence H − O/8.

name: Wobbe Index
description: Measures the interchangeability of fuel gases: gases with the same Wobbe index give the same heat through the same burner.
notes: Used when blending hydrogen or biomethane into gas grids.

name: Excess Air from Flue-Gas Oxygen
description: Estimates the excess combustion air from the oxygen measured in a boiler's flue gas.
notes: 3 % O₂ ≈ 17 % excess air; too much wastes heat up the stack.

name: Stirred Tank Reynolds Number
description: Gives the Reynolds number of a mixing tank; above about 10,000 flow is fully turbulent and the power number is constant.
notes: Uses rotational speed, not a velocity.

name: Concentration after Evaporation
description: Gives the solids fraction of a solution or food after evaporating water, from a solids mass balance.
notes: Used for juice concentration, sugar and milk powder.
